sub: Do you take God at His Word?
script: Before we begin, I want to make my purpose clear. My purpose is to help you know God. We are going to talk about creation, and some of what I say may challenge an assumption you have held for a long time. I want us to be able to examine those assumptions together. My authority today is not my own. Please do not believe something simply because Phil said it. Open your Bible. Look at the context. Ask whether the argument actually follows from the passage. Here is the question I want us to carry through this whole message: do you take God at His Word?

big:
My purpose is to
help you know God.
sub: Every misconception His Word corrects is a blessing.
script: We bring ideas about God from our upbringing, from the culture around us, and from people we admire. Sometimes we do not even realize those ideas are there. When Scripture corrects one of them, that is a blessing. It gives us the opportunity to know Him more faithfully. I care about creation because I care about the Creator. I care about what we mean when we say God is good, and about how the beginning of the Bible connects with the gospel. I also want you to know that disagreement with my chronology does not automatically place you outside Christ. We can examine serious disagreements while remembering who saves us.

left:
Belonging to Christ
Receiving His authority
right:
Seeking its approval
Accepting its authority
script: Pastor George’s message from John 15 helped me think about allegiance. Jesus tells His disciples that they do not belong to the world. Colossians describes rescue from darkness and transfer into the kingdom of the Son. That puts a serious question before us: where does our allegiance lie? Whose approval ultimately governs us? I do not mean that everyone who disagrees with Phil about Genesis belongs to the wrong kingdom. That would confuse my interpretation with Christ Himself. I mean that all of us, including me, need to ask whether we will submit to Christ when His Word challenges what our culture or our own circle expects us to say.

t: A real dichotomy or a false choice?
ref: Allegiance to Christ and restaurant preferences are different kinds of questions
script: Dichotomy is a useful word when there really are two mutually exclusive alternatives. But we can also manufacture a false choice. Imagine somebody asking whether you are a Chick-fil-A person or an In-N-Out person. Wait a minute. What happened to all the other restaurants? Ordinary preferences do not become a genuine either-or just because someone presents them that way. That matters in this conversation. Allegiance to Christ is serious. But a disagreement over the creation days is not automatically a choice between loving Jesus and hating Him. We need to identify the actual alternatives before we turn an argument into a spiritual loyalty test.

sub: Our reading remains accountable to the text.
script: I believe Scripture is authoritative. I also know that I can misunderstand a passage. Those two convictions belong together. Trusting God’s Word does not require me to pretend my first interpretation is incapable of correction. We read, we draw conclusions, and then we bring those conclusions back to the text. Have we respected the context? Have we allowed another passage to clarify this one? Have we imported something the passage does not actually say? That is what I mean by letting Scripture interpret Scripture. I am inviting you to examine my argument with that same care. If I mishandle a passage, I need to be corrected by it too.

sub: “I am the door” calls for understanding the image.
script: When Jesus says He is the door, taking Him seriously does not mean looking for hinges. It means listening to the image in its setting and understanding what He is teaching. A plain reading respects figures of speech, genre, and context. We need that same care in Genesis. I do not want to use literal as a shortcut that prevents us from reading thoughtfully. Neither do I want the presence of figurative language somewhere in the Bible to become permission to dismiss history wherever it becomes uncomfortable. Read the passage, read around it, and ask what kind of claim the author is actually making.

sub: What exactly do we mean by the word?
script: Let me say something that may surprise you. Evolution is an observable feature of living populations. Now, before anybody panics, let me explain what I mean. Heritable characteristics of populations change across generations. We observe variation, inheritance, and natural selection. I believe the God who made living creatures made them capable of adaptation. But people use the word evolution to mean several different things. Think about catholic in the Apostles’ Creed. There it refers to the universal church. If we miss a word’s meaning, we can misunderstand the whole statement. So before we argue, we should make sure we are arguing about the same claim.

ref: Definitions distinguish biological, historical, and philosophical claims
script: When I spoke with Ben about evolution, he thought first about stars and planets. Someone else hears the same word and pictures human ancestry. Those are different subjects. Cosmic development concerns the history of the universe. Biological evolution concerns changes in living populations and the ancestry of organisms. Abiogenesis concerns the origin of the first life. Philosophical naturalism makes a further claim about reality and the absence of a Creator. These subjects can connect in someone’s worldview, but they are not interchangeable. A Christian who accepts common ancestry has not therefore said that God does not exist. I disagree with that Christian’s reading of creation, but I must represent the position accurately.

t: Common ancestry is a branching claim
ref: Schematic of the scientific claim, not a dated family tree
script: That familiar picture of an ape gradually standing upright can give the wrong impression. The scientific claim is not that humans descended from the chimpanzees alive today. It is that humans and other living apes share ancestors. That is why a branching diagram is more accurate than a parade ending with a modern person. The broader common-ancestry claim extends across living things much further than this simple diagram shows. I reject universal common ancestry, but I do not help my argument by attacking a position scientists are not actually asserting. Understanding the claim fairly gives us a better starting point for asking where the evidence and the interpretation lead.

ref: U.S. adults, May 2024 Gallup survey. Percentages total 100.
script: This survey helps us see why definitions matter. In Gallup’s May 2024 survey, thirty-seven percent chose the view that God created humans in their present form within roughly the last ten thousand years. Thirty-four percent chose evolution guided by God. Twenty-four percent chose evolution without God’s involvement. Five percent gave no opinion. This is a survey of U.S. adults, not a worldwide survey, and these are 2024 results. Popularity does not determine truth. What the graph does show is that believing in God and accepting evolution are not mutually exclusive categories in people’s answers. We should understand that range before describing everyone on the other side as believing the same thing.

t: Order and the question of a mind
sub: What would you infer if you saw this on a beach?
ref: An illustration of design intuition, not a biological experiment
script: Imagine flying over an island and seeing SOS arranged on the beach. You would look for someone. The arrangement carries a meaning that makes you think of a mind. That illustration expresses why order and intelligibility draw my attention toward a Creator. But an illustration does not settle every question about biological mechanisms. Natural selection is not the same process as a tornado blowing through a scrap yard, and a messy house is not a scientific model of a population. I want to keep the intuition without pretending the analogy has done work it has not done. My strongest concern today is theological: what kind of original creation does Scripture describe?

left:
Could He create
in any amount of time?
right:
What did He make
and call very good?
script: The deepest issue for me is not whether God had enough power or enough time. He did not need six days, six seconds, or billions of years. His power is not the limitation. Here is the issue that concerns me: did He establish His original living world through a long history of animal suffering, disease, predation, and death before Adam sinned? When I imagine an animal starving before human rebellion, I ask how that fits with the completed creation God calls very good. I want to build that concern from the whole Bible. I do not want two words to carry an argument that needs several passages.

sub: Through Him. For Him.
script: Open your Bible at the beginning. God created the heavens and the earth. The universe belongs to Him. John tells us that all things came into being through the Word. Colossians tells us that all things were created through Christ and for Christ. Genesis describes the Spirit of God over the waters. We are speaking about the one eternal triune God, not three independent creators. And that means creation is not an unrelated preface before the Bible gets to Jesus. The One through whom all things were made is the One who comes to redeem. The beginning and the gospel belong to the same story.

t: Why I read six ordinary days
script: I believe Genesis describes six ordinary days. The repeated evenings and mornings matter to my reading. The numbered days matter. Exodus matters too, because it grounds Israel’s six days of labor and seventh-day Sabbath in God’s creation pattern. I find that connection compelling. I know Christians interpret the account differently, and we should discuss the actual text rather than assume everyone who differs is trying to escape it. My claim is that this reading fits the account and its connection with the Sabbath. God did not take six days because He was struggling to finish. The rhythm itself teaches us something about His completed work and His provision for His people.

ref: Genesis 1:3–31    Day 7 completes the pattern in Genesis 2:1–3
script: Notice the correspondences between the first three days and the next three. Light and darkness correspond with the lights governing day and night. Waters and sky correspond with sea creatures and birds. Land and vegetation correspond with land animals and humanity. These pairings help us pay attention to the account’s order. They do not, by themselves, prove or disprove a chronological reading. Also notice the details: the gathered seas are named on day three, and vegetation appears on day three. Day seven is a distinct culmination, not another pair. Let us walk through the days with room both for what the passage says and for questions it leaves us asking.

sub: The luminaries appear in the day-four account.
script: One thing that stops me here is the separation of light and darkness before the day-four account of the lights. I do not fully understand that. I want to be able to say so without treating my uncertainty as a defect in Scripture. The passage tells us what God does; it does not answer every physical question we can ask. The account also sounds to me as though it describes creation with attention to the earth, but that is an observation about the description, not proof of a technical viewpoint. Let us distinguish what is written from the model we build in our minds to picture it.

When I first read this, I pictured a water canopy or perhaps clouds. Then I kept reading about the lights in the expanse and the birds flying across it, and I began reconsidering what I was picturing. Is sky the best English description here? Are we thinking too narrowly if we insist on one modern physical category? I want Scripture to interpret Scripture. We can compare the Flood account and Psalm 148. But the comparison does not authorize us to claim that Genesis explicitly describes a vapor canopy that later collapsed. That would be a hypothesis. The useful starting point is the distinction the passage actually makes between the waters and the expanse.

sub:
A tree can give fruit
without the whole tree dying.
script: Here the land appears and vegetation bears seed and fruit. I love the provision in that picture. A fruit tree can feed a creature and continue growing, bearing again in another season. Animals can also disperse some seeds after eating fruit. There is beauty in that relationship. I am not saying every seed survives every animal, or that no plant cells die. Plants are living organisms. I am saying we should notice the distinction between plants given for food and the question of animal suffering and death. God’s power is not the limitation. The question is what kind of provision He describes in the world He calls good.

sub: Signs. Seasons. Days. Years.
script: If you have the opportunity to stand under a truly dark sky, do it. Pictures do not replace that experience for me. Look through a telescope if you can. The heavens draw my attention to the glory of their Maker. Genesis describes lights marking times and illuminating the earth. The Moon reflects sunlight, and that gives me a devotional illustration: we ought to reflect the light we receive rather than behave as though it originates in us. That is an application, not a hidden Hebrew argument. The English similarity between sun and son does not establish the meaning of Genesis. The wonder is already there without making the illustration prove more than it can.

t: Day 5: life fills the waters and sky
sub: Sea creatures and birds receive His blessing.
script: The waters teem with living creatures and birds fly above the earth. Notice the blessing. God addresses His creatures with fruitfulness and multiplication. He cares about the life He has made. This develops the connection with the waters and sky described earlier. I also notice the repeated references to kinds and goodness. But I do not want to assume that the word kinds automatically corresponds to a particular modern scientific rank, such as species or family. We should read the word carefully rather than use it as a shortcut. The movement I want us to see is God creating, blessing, and providing a world that fills with life.

sub: Made in God’s image
disclosure: AI illustration of a young-earth creationist interpretation
script: Genesis describes land animals and then humanity made in God’s image. That distinction matters. Our worth and accountability are grounded in our relationship to our Maker. I have included this imagined scene because I read the land animals and humans as belonging to the same creation day. The picture expresses that young-earth interpretation. It is not a recovered photograph or independent evidence of humans living with non-avian dinosaurs. The mainstream scientific chronology places those dinosaurs long before humans. My purpose here is to make my reading visible while being honest about the difference between an illustration of a belief and evidence that establishes it.

sub:
A picture can illustrate a view.
It cannot establish its history.
disclosure: AI illustration. Human–dinosaur coexistence shown as Phil’s interpretation.
script: Dinosaurs are exciting. Their size and variety make us stop and look. I want that wonder in this presentation, but I also want us to know exactly what we are claiming. Genesis does not use the modern word dinosaur. Identifying Job’s Behemoth or Leviathan with a particular extinct species is debated. An artist can show a human beside a giant animal, but the artwork is not the evidence. If we are going to discuss fossils, chronology, or Job’s creatures in detail, we need to examine those arguments on their own terms. For this devotional, keep the central connection clear: I believe God made the land animals and humanity, and I want to understand that claim faithfully.

Do not let the chapter number stop you. Genesis 2:1–3 completes the creation account. God finishes His work, ceases from that work, and blesses the seventh day. This is not God recovering because He has run out of strength. Isaiah reminds us that He does not faint or grow weary. The rest marks completion. Exodus then draws on this pattern for Israel’s work and Sabbath. I appreciate that God gives His people a rhythm. We are creatures. We work, and we need rest. His completed creation gives us something to receive with gratitude rather than treating our lives as an endless attempt to prove that everything depends on us.

sub: His completed creation receives His approval.
script: Here is the assessment I keep returning to: very good. God looks at everything He has made and approves His completed creation. What belongs inside that declaration? I believe it is difficult to place animal starvation, disease, predation, and death before human rebellion and then call that the means by which God established His original good world. But I do not want to pretend these two words settle every question by themselves. A tree being good does not mean the tree has kept the commandments. Goodness in a created thing and moral righteousness in a person are related but distinct questions. Let the food provisions and the wider biblical story help us examine the claim.

left:
Plants for humanity
Green plants for animals
script: Compare these provisions. In Genesis 1 God gives plants as food to people and green plants to the animals described there as having life. After the Flood, Genesis 9 explicitly permits Noah to eat animals, with the restriction about blood following. The contrast deserves our attention. It supports the question I am raising about the original world. At the same time, the later permission does not make every act of eating meat sinful. You cannot eat an In-N-Out burger without the death of a cow, but that is not the same question as whether animal death was part of God’s original completed creation. Keep the settings and the claims distinct.

ref: Schematic comparison, not a scaled scientific timeline
script: This is the central contrast in my argument. In the mainstream evolutionary history, animal suffering and death precede humans by a very long time. Christians who accept that history may understand it within God’s providence. In my reading, God’s original creation is good, human rebellion brings the Fall, and animal suffering and death belong to the fallen world. I want us to examine how these readings connect creation, the curse, and restoration. The diagram does not establish either account merely by arranging labels. It identifies where the disagreement lies. I believe the whole-Bible pattern supports my conclusion, while recognizing that Christians dispute how far particular passages extend.

sub: The world after the Fall carries the consequences of sin.
script: Genesis 3 describes rebellion against the Creator. The issue is not that people lacked enough information to win a debate. They disobeyed God. Judgment follows, the ground is cursed, toil becomes painful, and the man is told he will return to dust. The account changes the way we understand the world we inhabit. Our present experience is not simply the original creation continuing untouched. There is beauty, but there is also rupture. There is provision, but also pain. As we read onward, we should pay attention to the connection between human rebellion and the world’s brokenness without claiming that Genesis answers every question about the chronology of all evil.

Romans 5 connects sin entering through one man with death spreading to humanity. Paul is explaining our relationship to Adam and our need for Christ. This passage matters enormously to the gospel. Adam’s disobedience and Christ’s obedience are not disconnected ideas. But notice the precision: Romans 5 directly discusses human sin and human death. It does not explicitly list every animal species. If I apply the wider argument to animal mortality, I need to explain the additional biblical connections. The strong point we must not lose is the one Paul does make: humanity needs the righteousness and life that come through Christ. We cannot repair Adam’s problem by congratulating ourselves on our own goodness.

sub: Creation’s bondage does not have the final word.
script: Romans 8 widens our attention to creation itself. Paul describes futility, groaning, and the hope of liberation from corruption. He connects that hope with the revealing of God’s children and the redemption of our bodies. That gives us a way to look honestly at suffering without treating it as the last truth about the world. The groaning is real. The hope is real too. This is one of the passages I bring into my larger argument about the Fall and creation’s brokenness. I do not want to isolate one verse and force it to answer everything. I want us to hear the movement from bondage toward the freedom God promises.

big:
Death is an enemy
Christ defeats.
sub: His resurrection is the firstfruits of His people’s resurrection.
script: First Corinthians 15 calls death an enemy. Paul places its defeat within the victory of the risen Christ and the resurrection of His people. This is not a small detail attached to an origins discussion. It is Christian hope. Death does not get the final word over those who belong to Jesus. That is one reason the place of death in the original creation concerns me. I see a movement in Scripture in which Christ overcomes what destroys and corrupts. I want to understand the beginning in the light of that promised victory. And I want our discussion to lead toward worship of the risen Savior rather than ending with a clever argument about the past.

Creation. Rebellion. Curse. Redemption. Resurrection. Restoration. These are connected movements in the biblical story. God creates. People rebel. Judgment and curse follow. God acts to redeem through Christ. Christ rises, and His people will rise. The promised end includes the removal of death and the curse. I believe this pattern helps us examine the place of suffering and death in the beginning. It also keeps us from treating Genesis as disposable background. The beginning matters because the same Creator is working toward the promised end. But keep the gospel at the center: the story reaches us as people who need rescue, not merely as observers who need an interesting explanation.

t: What does this say about God?
script: We have reached the heart of why this matters to me. What does our account of creation say about the God who made it? Scripture reveals His holiness, goodness, mercy, justice, wisdom, and love. I do not want to invent a version of goodness that simply mirrors my preferences. I want to ask how the Creator reveals Himself. When I picture animal suffering before human rebellion, I struggle to reconcile that with the original completed good creation. That is my conviction. I am inviting you to examine the biblical argument, not simply to share my emotional reaction. God’s character is the reason the question deserves more than a quick dismissal.

sub: God can bring good through suffering.
script: I need to make an important distinction here. I am not saying God can never permit suffering for a good purpose. Look at the cross. The people who crucified Jesus acted wickedly, and yet their wickedness did not defeat God’s saving purpose. God brings good through suffering. Christians also know that trials can produce endurance. My question concerns the original creation before the rebellion described in Genesis. We must not confuse God redeeming suffering in a fallen world with a claim that suffering itself is the original good or final goal. Keep that distinction clear so we do not make my creation argument say something much broader and less careful than I intend.

Am I saying every death in this fallen world is a moral evil? No. God’s judgment is righteous. Ezekiel calls the wicked to turn and live and says God takes no pleasure in their death. We can affirm justice without celebrating death itself as our final good. Genesis 9 also permits animals for food. That is a different question from cruelty, and a different question from original creation. Here are the distinctions I want us to keep: what belonged to the world God originally called very good, what God justly judges after rebellion, and what He permits for food in the fallen world. Keeping these separate strengthens the argument rather than weakening it.

ref: Adam: Genesis 5:5    Noah: Genesis 9:29    Shem: Genesis 11:10–11
script: We should also examine the way we dismiss ancient people. Genesis records Adam’s lifespan as nine hundred thirty years, Noah’s as nine hundred fifty, and Shem’s as six hundred in total. I take these as accounts of real people. Imagine the experience a person could accumulate across centuries. That is a possibility worth considering. Scripture does not give us their IQ scores or a medical mechanism for their longevity. So I am not using these bars to prove that everyone then was more intelligent than everyone now. I am using them to challenge our habit of assuming ancient means foolish. And across those long lives, there is still a sobering reality: death comes.

left:
How long has someone
believed it?
right:
What reasons and
evidence support it?
ref: The age of a claim does not settle its truth
script: We have remarkable tools and accumulated knowledge. That does not make us automatically wiser about God. We should not assume an older belief is false simply because it is old, or that a new idea is true simply because it sounds modern. The reverse error is possible too. A claim does not become true because it has a long tradition behind it. I want us to examine the reasons. When we read Genesis, let us avoid treating its people as fools merely because they lived long ago. Our phones may be newer. That does not mean our instincts about the Creator are beyond correction. Humility belongs to serious inquiry, including Christian inquiry.

sub: Lewis. Augustine. Your pastor. Phil.
script: I admire C. S. Lewis. That does not make every conclusion he reached my final authority. In The Problem of Pain he considers animal suffering before human beings, including a speculative prehuman evil behind it. We should represent that fairly, even when we disagree. Augustine also shows that disagreement about creation days did not begin with Darwin. Aquinas describes his understanding of simultaneous creation and non-successive days. I disagree with that reading, but it deserves accurate description. The lesson is not to stop learning from thoughtful Christians. It is to remember that admiration does not settle interpretation. Not Lewis. Not Augustine. Not your pastor. And certainly not me.
sources:
C. S. Lewis, The Problem of Pain, chapter IX: https://www.gutenberg.ca/ebooks/lewiscs-problemofpain/lewiscs-problemofpain-00-h.html
Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I.74.2, reporting Augustine: https://www.newadvent.org/summa/1074.htm

big:
Am I submitting
to my Creator?
sub: A correct argument cannot substitute for obedience.
script: Now I want this to get personal. It is possible to defend six days passionately and still resist what God says about your own sin. In Mark 10, the rich man calls Jesus good teacher. Jesus turns his attention to God’s goodness and exposes the allegiance he will not surrender. He wants eternal life, but will he follow Jesus? That question reaches us too. Romans 3 says all have sinned. Psalm 139 reminds us that God knows the public self and the private self. He knows the selfishness beneath an impressive act and the bitterness we keep explaining away. I cannot argue my way out of that. Neither can you.

sub: The Creator came to save.
script: This is why the devotional must end with the gospel. The God who made us is the God against whom we have sinned. Jesus Christ lived the righteous life we have not lived. He bore sin at the cross. He died, and He rose bodily from the grave. Death did not have the final word over Him, and it will not have the final word over those who belong to Him. Romans 6 contrasts sin’s wages with God’s gift of eternal life in Christ. We need a Savior. The answer to our sin is not a more impressive public image or a more polished debate. It is Jesus Christ, crucified and risen.

left:
My goodness
My performance
My arguments
right:
His righteousness
His saving work
His promise
script: Salvation is not a reward for understanding every chapter of Genesis. It is God’s gift of grace received through faith in Christ. So if you have never turned to Him, repent and trust Him. Do not rest your hope in church attendance, your own goodness, or your ability to win an argument. Rest it in Christ. And if you belong to Him, remember that your acceptance rests in Him. God does not become unaware of His children’s sins. We still confess them. But there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. Good works grow from His grace. They do not become the price we pay to purchase it.

sub:
God with His people.
Death and mourning removed.
script: Our hope reaches beyond forgiveness alone. Christ will raise His people. God will dwell with them. Death, mourning, and the curse will not rule forever. The promised future is not merely that we stop asking questions about the past. It is life with our Creator in a world no longer broken by sin. That hope changes how we face suffering now. We can grieve without pretending death is harmless, and we can trust without pretending we understand every detail. The One through whom all things were made is faithful to complete His saving work. This is the hope I want us to carry from the beginning of Scripture toward its promised end.

t: Do you take God at His Word?
sub:
Bring Him the belief you never questioned.
Bring Him the command you keep avoiding.
script: Here is the response I am asking for. Submit yourself to God’s Word. Bring Him the belief you have never questioned. Bring Him the command you keep avoiding. Bring Him the part of your life where you want forgiveness but resist His authority. Do not take my word for everything we have discussed. Open Genesis. Read the passages around the verses. Bring your questions. If I have handled a passage wrongly, show me. I need to submit to His Word too. Let us pray that God gives us humility, corrects our errors, deepens our trust in Christ, and makes us willing to obey. The question is whether we will hear Him and respond.

ref: A place for honest questions and careful reading
script: I would like to hear your questions. We do not need to pretend we have resolved every issue. Which passage would you like to examine more closely? Where did an interpretive step need more explanation? What do you understand very good to mean in its context? How do you connect Genesis 3, Romans 8, and the promised removal of the curse? We can also ask a more personal question: where do we rely on our own goodness instead of God’s grace? Please feel free to disagree and show us the text behind your answer. I want a conversation that helps us know God and understand His Word more faithfully.
